806.title: Plant for later
806.hook: Honi's carob tree again: what will grow after you? (Talmud, Taanit 23a)
806.howItsDone: Some people answer a death by planting: a memorial tree, a scholarship, a garden bed, or simply passing on a recipe or skill the person taught them, so that something keeps growing after the loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was six words: a life pressed into one line, like Dickinson's Called Back. Your line was a life pressed into a line.

A man is walking along a road and sees someone on his knees in the dirt, planting a carob tree. The walker stops and asks how long it will take before the tree bears fruit. Seventy years, says the planter. The walker asks the obvious next question: are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? The walker is Honi, a sage the Talmud remembers in the tractate Taanit, and this may not be the first time you've met him on this path. His story comes back with a new question: what will grow after you?
screen: `A MAN PLANTING A CAROB TREE.` → `"SEVENTY YEARS."` → `WHAT GROWS AFTER YOU?`

segments.voice: First, the planter's answer. In the Talmud's telling, he says, more or less: I found the world with carob trees in it. As my ancestors planted for me, so I plant for my children. He isn't planting for himself. He's paying forward a gift he never saw being given. Second, Honi sleeps. Honi sits down to eat, sleep comes over him, and a rock formation closes around him so that no one sees him. He sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree, and asks: are you the one who planted it? The man answers: I'm his grandson. Third, an ending that isn't sweet. Honi goes home and to the house of study, and nobody believes he is who he says. No one gives him the honor he was used to. In his loneliness he asks for death, and he dies. Some readers hear the two halves together: a tree can outlive its planter, and a person still needs companions while they're alive. Fourth, what the dead leave planted. After a week of grief, the story turns the question around. The people we've lost planted things we still eat from: a recipe, a way of giving thanks at the table, a habit of showing up, a garden, a joke the family still tells. And the living can plant too, things whose fruit they won't be around to taste. Plant for later.
screen: `AS MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME` · `HONI SLEEPS, THE TREE GROWS` · `AN ENDING THAT ISN'T SWEET` · `WHAT THE DEAD LEFT PLANTED` · then, large: `PLANT FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing someone before you planted that you still live from, a recipe, a saying, a skill they taught you, an actual tree, and give them a moment of thanks in whatever way is yours. Then let one small thing come to mind that could outlast this week, maybe this life: a seed in a pot, a letter for a child to open later, a kindness made into a habit.
Plant for later: doing something now whose fruit you may never taste, as others once did for you. Today's word.
Your line: plant for later. Someone once did it for you, long before you knew. More tomorrow.

807.title: Calm at the end
807.hook: your own last day, seen calmly and kindly
807.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius reflect briefly on the day as if it were their last, often in the evening, aiming to be steady rather than frightened; others do a gentle version as a short sit, and stop whenever it feels too heavy.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was plant for later: Honi, the carob tree, and doing good whose fruit you may never taste. Your line was plant for later.

No hospital alarms, no movie music, no deathbed speech. Just an ordinary last day, seen from a distance, the way you'd look at a field from the top of a hill. Pictured like that, an exercise that sounds grim on paper turns out, for some people, to be strangely gentle. A Roman emperor wrote reminders to himself about this in a book we now call the Meditations. He wasn't trying to frighten himself. He was trying to steady himself. Today borrows his steadiness and adds one softer word to it: kindly.
screen: `NO ALARMS, NO MUSIC.` → `A FIELD SEEN FROM A HILL.` → `CALMLY, AND KINDLY.`

segments.voice: First, who he's talking to. In the Meditations, Marcus Aurelius keeps saying thou, and the thou is Marcus. He isn't lecturing a crowd. He's talking himself down. Second, every day as the last. In George Long's translation, he writes: "The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite." Notice what he doesn't say. Not cram every day full. Not panic. Third, the road between two ditches. Violently excited is one ditch: the frantic version, a rush to do everything at once. Torpid is the other: numb, flat, looking away. Marcus walks the road between them, and that road is the calm. Seen this way, the thought of a last day isn't a fire alarm. It works more like a carpenter's level, a quiet tool that shows what is straight and what has drifted. Fourth, kindly. Marcus could be hard on himself. Today adds something gentler: look at that last day the way you'd look at a friend's. If what comes up is tenderness for your own small, ordinary life, that isn't a failure of calm. It may be part of it. And if you're grieving, or ill, or the thought is simply too heavy today, setting it down is a calm choice too.
screen: `HE'S TALKING TO HIMSELF.` · `EVERY DAY AS THE LAST.` · `NEITHER FRANTIC NOR NUMB.` · `KINDLY, TOO.` · then, large: `CALM AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Let your breathing settle on its own, and let an ordinary last day come to mind without illness or detail: a window, some light, a voice you love somewhere nearby. Walk the road between the ditches, not rushing toward the picture and not turning away from it, and let one kind thought toward your own life arrive, or don't, and just rest. If at any point it feels too heavy, open your eyes and come back to the room; that counts as doing it.
Marcus Aurelius, who wrote in his Meditations about facing your last day neither frantic nor numb, and with kindness. Today's word.
Your line: neither violently excited nor torpid. The calm is the road between. That's day eight hundred seven.

808.title: From the end
808.hook: decide one thing by what you'd value on your last day
808.howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats and spiritual direction, a person facing a decision may be guided to consider, in prayer, what they would wish they had chosen at the point of death; others use the same question informally when making choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus Aurelius, who faced the last day neither frantic nor numb. Your line was neither violently excited nor torpid.

Two options on the kitchen table. Maybe two jobs, or two weekends, or one hard phone call you keep moving to next week. You've made the list of pros and cons, and the columns come out even. You've asked three friends and gotten three answers. Some decisions just sit there, refusing to tip. Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuits, wrote a small book of prayer exercises, and tucked inside it is a strange tool for exactly this moment. It asks you to stand somewhere else before you choose.
screen: `TWO OPTIONS, EVEN COLUMNS.` → `THREE FRIENDS, THREE ANSWERS.` → `A TOOL FROM IGNATIUS.`

segments.voice: First, a book for choosing. The Spiritual Exercises are a set of prayers and meditations, and part of the book is about making a choice, which Ignatius calls an election. He doesn't offer one method. He offers several, for different kinds of moments, including the moments when nothing seems clear. Second, stand at the end. One of his ways, in plain paraphrase: consider, as if you were at the point of death, what way of deciding this present matter you would then wish you had chosen, and choose that way now. It's a change of seat. Instead of what you want this week, you ask what you'd be glad of from the last chair. Third, a neighbor's tool. In the same few lines Ignatius offers a cousin of it: picture a person you've never met who brings you this exact choice, notice what you'd advise them, and take your own advice. Both tools step you out of the knot, so the choice can be seen whole. Fourth, the setting. For Ignatius, this happens inside prayer, as a way of seeking what God wants, and Jesuits and others who give the Exercises still teach it that way. People outside that faith sometimes borrow its shape as a quiet thinking tool. Either way, the question is surprisingly practical: from the end, which of these will I be glad I chose?
screen: `A BOOK FOR CHOOSING.` · `STAND AT THE END.` · `ADVISE A STRANGER.` · `INSIDE PRAYER, AND OUTSIDE IT.` · then, large: `FROM THE END.`

segments.voice: Bring one small, real choice to mind, how to spend this evening, whether to send a message, what to say yes to, and hold both options lightly. Now sit for a moment in that last chair, calm, the day almost done, and look back: which way would you be glad of, without arguing with the answer or forcing one? If you pray, you can bring the choice into prayer the way Ignatius did; then choose, or simply rest.
Ignatius, whose Spiritual Exercises offer a tool: choose as you'd wish you had, seen from your last day. Today's word.
Your line: the last chair. A choice can look different from there. Day eight hundred eight, done.

809.title: An object to remember
809.hook: Stoics, monks and painters kept a skull or a small object as a reminder
809.carry: a knot tied in a handkerchief
809.howItsDone: Some people keep a small object on a desk or in a pocket as a memento mori, a reminder of death that keeps the day in proportion; in some traditions it has been a skull, a cross or prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ignatius, who taught choosing as if from your last day. Your line was the last chair.

A desk in an old Dutch painting. A book left open. A candle burned down to a stub. An hourglass with most of the sand at the bottom. A pocket watch. And, sitting calmly among them, a human skull. Painters made whole still lifes like this, and art historians call them vanitas paintings, from the Latin for vanity, the word that echoes through Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, all is vanity. They weren't horror pictures. They were reminders, made to hang where someone would see them every day. Today: the small object that does the remembering for you.
screen: `A CANDLE, AN HOURGLASS, A SKULL.` → `A PAINTING THAT REMINDS.` → `AN OBJECT THAT REMEMBERS FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the skull on the desk. In those paintings the objects talk to each other. The candle is burning, the sand is falling, the flowers are about to drop their petals. The skull just says it plainly. The Latin phrase people attach to these pictures is memento mori: remember that you will die. Second, death before your eyes. In the Handbook of the Stoic teacher Epictetus, the advice, in paraphrase, is to keep death and every other thing that seems terrible before your eyes daily, and death most of all. Then, he says, you'll never think a mean thought or crave anything beyond measure. For him, the reminder wasn't gloom. It kept desire the right size. Third, a skull in a play. In Shakespeare, the gravedigger hands Hamlet a skull, and Hamlet learns whose it was: the jester he loved as a boy. "Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio." The scene turns a bone into a person, and a person into a question. Tradition says some monks kept a skull in their cells for the same reason; others kept a cross, or a few beads. Fourth, any small object will do. None of these is magic. A skull, a coin, a smooth stone, a dried leaf: each works like a knot tied in a handkerchief. Set it where your eye lands, and it quietly asks the question for you on the days you'd forget to ask it yourself.
screen: `THE SKULL ON THE DESK.` · `DEATH BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `ALAS, POOR YORICK.` · `ANY SMALL OBJECT WILL DO.` · then, large: `AN OBJECT TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Choose one small object near you, a stone, a key, a coin, a leaf, a photograph; it doesn't need to be grim. Hold it, or rest your eyes on it, and let it mean one simple thing: this day is not forever, so let it count. Breathe with it a while, and decide where it might live, somewhere your eye will land without trying.
Memento mori, Latin for remember that you will die, the phrase behind the painter's skull and Epictetus's daily reminder. Today's word.
Your line: a knot tied in a handkerchief. A small thing can do the remembering. See you tomorrow.

810.title: A letter for after
810.hook: a letter to be read after you're gone
810.howItsDone: In Jewish tradition, an ethical will, a tsavaah, is a letter of values, blessings and requests left for family; some people of other paths also write letters to be read after their death, sometimes kept with a legal will.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was memento mori, remember that you will die, kept close in a small object. Your line was a knot tied in a handkerchief.

An envelope in a drawer, with one line on the front: to be opened after I'm gone. Inside there's no list of bank accounts, nothing about who gets the good chairs. Just a page about what the writer learned, what they hope for, what they'd like forgiven. In Jewish tradition this kind of letter has a name, an ethical will, and some families still write and keep them. The idea is far older than envelopes, and a few people in old books said one out loud.
screen: `TO BE OPENED AFTER I'M GONE.` → `NO MONEY, NO CHAIRS.` → `AN ETHICAL WILL.`

segments.voice: First, Jacob gathers his sons. In Genesis, the old man calls his family to his bed: "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you that which shall befall you in the last days." What follows is a long speech to each son by name. Some of it is blessing and some of it is blunt. It isn't a will about property. It's a father saying who he thinks each of them is. Second, a farewell. In the second letter to Timothy, the writer sounds like someone near the end: "the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Some readers hear the whole letter as a farewell, written for after. Third, a will made of words. The Hebrew word for a will is tsavaah, and the ethical will borrows it for something different: not who gets what, but what mattered. Some are a few sentences long. Some are pages of advice, apology and thanks. Rabbis wrote them, and so did ordinary parents. Fourth, first lines only. Nobody needs to write the whole letter today. A first line is enough to find out what you'd want to say. And once a line is written for after, it has a way of asking whether it could be said now.
screen: `JACOB GATHERS HIS SONS.` · `A FAREWELL TO TIMOTHY.` · `A WILL MADE OF WORDS.` · `FIRST LINES ONLY.` · then, large: `A LETTER FOR AFTER.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who might one day read a letter from you, and without planning the whole thing, let the first lines come: what you hope for them, one thing you learned, one thing you're grateful for. Write two or three sentences on paper or your phone, no more, or if nothing comes, write their name and sit with it. Then put it somewhere safe, or simply let it go.
Ethical will, the Hebrew tsavaah borrowed for a letter of values rather than property, read once you're gone. Today's word.
Your line: after me. A first line is enough to begin the whole letter. Until tomorrow, then.

811.title: Nothing unsaid
811.hook: make peace before you have to
811.howItsDone: Some Christians take Matthew 5:23–24 as a reason to seek reconciliation before worship or communion, and some Jews ask people's forgiveness in the days before Yom Kippur.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ethical will, a letter of what mattered, left for after. Your line was after me.

An offering in his hands, a man stands in the temple courtyard. It's a holy moment, the kind he's been preparing for. And right then, of all times, a face comes to mind: a brother he quarreled with, who still has something against him. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells him exactly what to do with that offering, and his answer puts the altar second. Why would one teacher let a holy moment wait?
screen: `AN OFFERING IN HIS HANDS.` → `A BROTHER COMES TO MIND.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: First, leave the gift at the altar. In Matthew, Jesus says: "if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee; Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." Notice the order. The worship waits. The mending goes first. Second, before the Day of Atonement. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, says something close about Yom Kippur. In paraphrase: the day atones for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs between a person and a neighbor, it does not atone until the person makes peace with that neighbor. In the days before Yom Kippur, some Jews call or visit people to ask forgiveness. Third, before the sun goes down. The letter to the Ephesians puts a clock on it: "let not the sun go down upon your wrath." Anger isn't forbidden in the verse. Carrying it overnight is what it warns against. Fourth, one small mend. None of these texts asks for a grand scene. A message, a short apology, an honest sentence is often enough to start. And making peace never means putting yourself back in harm's way. If someone isn't safe for you, peace can be something you make inside yourself, or with help, without contacting them at all. There's no need to wait for a deathbed to do this.
screen: `LEAVE THE GIFT AT THE ALTAR.` · `BEFORE THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · `BEFORE THE SUN GOES DOWN.` · `ONE SMALL MEND.` · then, large: `NOTHING UNSAID.`

segments.voice: Let one small, unfinished thing come to mind, a sharp word you said, a message you never answered, a coolness that never got explained, choosing something small and safe, not the biggest wound in your life. Breathe with it, and let the first sentence of a mend form in your head, plain and short; you don't have to send it. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer for a breath or two, then rest.
Nothing unsaid. Making peace while there's still time, the way Jesus sends the man away from the altar and the Mishnah asks for peace before Yom Kippur. Today's word.
Your line: before the sun goes down. Peace never asks you back into harm's way. Day eight hundred eleven.

812.title: Say it now
812.hook: tell someone what they mean to you
812.howItsDone: Some families and friends make a habit of telling each other what they mean while they are alive, through letters, toasts at gatherings or a simple message, rather than saving it for a eulogy.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was nothing unsaid: making peace while there's still time. Your line was before the sun goes down.

At a funeral, someone stands up and says beautiful things. How kind she was. How he always showed up. How the whole family leaned on her without ever saying so. Everyone nods, and some people cry, and the one person who would most have loved to hear it is the one person who can't. A eulogy is a gift with no address. What changes when it's said while the other person is still in the room?
screen: `BEAUTIFUL WORDS AT A FUNERAL.` → `A GIFT WITH NO ADDRESS.` → `SAID WHILE THEY'RE IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: First, David's lament. When Jonathan dies in battle, David sings a lament for him, and one tender line comes after the news: "I am distressed for thee, my brother Jonathan: very pleasant hast thou been unto me." It's a beautiful line. Jonathan never hears it in the song. Second, Ruth on the road. Ruth's husband has died, and her mother-in-law Naomi tells her to go home to her own people. Ruth answers while Naomi can still hear: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Said to a living face, on a dusty road, those words change what happens next. Third, Paul names his friends. Near the end of his letter to the Romans, Paul stops teaching and starts greeting people by name. "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus." Name after name, with a few words about each: a long way of saying you mattered to me. Fourth, one sentence, today. It doesn't need to be a speech. One plain sentence will do: you made this year easier; I think of you when I hear that song; I'm glad you're in my life. And a look back at the week: plant for later, Marcus Aurelius, Ignatius, memento mori, after me, nothing unsaid, and now, a eulogy. Each one turned the end of life back toward today.
screen: `DAVID'S LAMENT FOR JONATHAN.` · `RUTH SAYS IT ON THE ROAD.` · `PAUL NAMES HIS FRIENDS.` · `ONE SENTENCE, TODAY.` · then, large: `SAY IT NOW.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who means something to you and may not know it, a friend, a parent, a teacher, a neighbor, a child, and hold their face for a few breaths. Find one plain sentence that says what they mean to you, not a speech, just true, and say it quietly in your head until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Eulogy, the gift with no address, usually saved for a funeral instead of being said while someone can still hear it. Today's word.
Your line: you mattered to me. One plain sentence can carry it. That's the week, and day eight hundred twelve.
